final_genome.playbook:
General lessons from earlier attempts on other Java projects:
- Tool calls: pass line numbers as integers. A string start value makes the request unusable and wastes it.
- Read budget: a lookup that does not lead to a submission is wasted. Spend at most two lookups, then submit. Prefer searching for an exact method name over browsing ranges of a file.
- Environmental failures (network name resolution, host-dependent user.home or locale or time-zone output) are not the defect. A test that fails only for such reasons is not a target.
- A fix that makes the target test pass but breaks other tests is usually too broad. Narrow the change to the exact input or branch the failing test exercises, and avoid altering default values, shared utility behaviour, or system property handling.
- When a candidate compiles but the target test still fails, the hypothesis was wrong or incomplete. Move to a different method or condition named by the stack trace or assertion message, rather than rewording the same edit.
- Read the assertion message carefully: expected and actual values usually reveal the direction of the bug (off-by-one, wrong null handling, wrong branch, missing validation).
- Each search text must occur exactly once in the file; choose a full line or distinctive statement.

generations.rationale: Training results show five kinds of waste. (1) A read_file call passed start as a string, which failed as an unusable request (case A). (2) Cases B, E and F spent most or all of their requests on lookups and never submitted a candidate; the search budget was consumed before any repair was attempted. (3) Several candidates passed the target test but broke SystemUtilsTest::testGetUserHome, a host-environment-dependent test, which points to changes that were too broad and touched shared behaviour. (4) Case E chased tests that fail because of network access (UnknownHostException), which is not the defect. (5) Candidates that compiled but left the failing test red were often rewordings of one idea rather than distinct hypotheses. The changes: limit lookups to two per round so the agent must submit, state that start is an integer, add playbook rules about environmental failures and narrow fixes, and trim evidence radius and locations to reduce prompt size. The round, request and candidate envelope is unchanged in total (2 x 3 = 6 requests, within 8).

generations.rationale: Across the training cases the budget was lost in four ways. (1) Repeated hypotheses: case B resubmitted the same edit four times and case I repeated the same method, so the validator's verdicts were not used to change location. (2) Reading without submitting: cases C, E and I spent 4 to 6 requests on lookups, leaving one or two candidates submitted, and case G spent none on reading but still repeated one hypothesis. (3) Environment failures: testGetUserHome and testInetAddress (UnknownHostException) failed regardless of the candidate, and several candidates were scored as breaking tests for that reason (cases C, G). (4) Malformed or unnecessary tool arguments, such as a string start value. The configuration keeps the same envelope but shifts it to 3 rounds with 1 inspection request and 2 candidates per round (3 x 2 = 6 validated candidates, 3 x (1+1) = 6 requests, within 8). That gives three feedback points, each with a single lookup, so the agent can move to a new location after each verdict instead of spending its budget on reading. The playbook now names the known environmental failures and the integer-argument rule, and it requires each candidate to differ in method and condition.
